claim: The share of covers showing someone at least partially unclothed fell from 29.8% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023.

source: In 2011 and 2012, about a third of the covers still had someone who was at least partially unclothed — almost always the man, alone or with a clothed lover.
claim: Across 2011 and 2012, 34.1% of covers showed someone at least partially unclothed.

source: In 2011 and 2012, about a third of the covers still had someone who was at least partially unclothed — almost always the man, alone or with a clothed lover.

source: While the overall rate for covers featuring some state of undress remained over a quarter of titles, the rate for unclothed women peaked in 2015 at 11%.
claim: From 2013 to 2015, the share of covers with someone at least partially unclothed stayed above a quarter of titles each year (27.7%, 27.5%, 27.3%).

source: the rate for unclothed women peaked in 2015 at 11%
claim: The share of covers with a partially unclothed woman was highest in 2015, at 10.9%.

source: By 2016, only 18% of covers had someone unclothed, falling consistently over the next few years to 10% or less from 2019 on.
claim: In 2016, 17.6% of covers showed someone partially unclothed; the shares for 2019 through 2023 were 9.0%, 10.2%, 5.9%, 6.7% and 2.6%.

source: In 2011 and 2012, there were just 7 illustrated covers of the 169 that made Publishers Weekly’s list.

source: from less than 10% of covers featuring people of color in the 2010s, doubled to over 20% in the 2020s
claim: Covers with at least one person of color made up 5.7% of the 2010s covers and 26.8% of the 2020s covers.

source: Annually between 2016 and 2019, covers with people of color accounted for less than a tenth of all featured covers.
claim: From 2016 to 2019, the yearly share of covers with a person of color was 5.6%, 4.1%, 5.0% and 7.2%.

source: In 2020, something drastically changed. That year, 20% of romance novels featured by Publishers Weekly had characters of color on the cover.
claim: In 2020, 20.3% of covers featured a person of color.

source: 39% of the ones the magazine featured — had characters of color on the cover
claim: In 2022, 38.7% of the featured covers had a person of color.

source: The share of racially diverse covers declined back down to 22% in 2023.
claim: The share of covers with a person of color fell from 38.7% in 2022 to 22.2% in 2023.

source: In 2012 in particular, 7 of 8 books that had Black protagonists on the cover were published by Kimani Romance.
claim: In 2012, 7 of the 8 covers with a person of color were published by Kimani Romance.

source: Many of those that did had covers with the signature red banner of Kimani Romance, an imprint of Harlequin that specifically published African-American romance stories, a first for a major publishing house.
claim: Among the 55 covers with a person of color from 2011 to 2019, 16 were published by Kimani.
code: l[(l['year'] <= 2019) & (l['Has POC'] == True)].assign(period='2011-2019').groupby('period')['publisher'].agg(total='size', kimani=lambda s: s.str.contains('Kimani', case=False).sum())

source: The contemporaneity of the trends mean that people of color tend to be depicted in illustrated pop art rather than seen realistically or sexually.
claim: Covers with a person of color were illustrated 52.7% of the time, versus 22.3% of covers without a person of color.
